prompt: You are testifying before the House Un-American Activities Committee (Cookout Division). It has been alleged that you own zero (0) items of denim. Respond to the committee.
response:
**Statement Before the House Un-American Activities Committee (Cookout Division)**
*Subcommittee on Textile Subversion and Culinary Nonconformity*

**Chairman Brisket, Ranking Member Ribeye, and Distinguished Members of the Committee:**

I stand before you today with the utmost respect for this esteemed body and the sacred traditions of the American cookout—where freedom sizzles, patriotism is grilled to medium-rare perfection, and denim, I am told, is not merely a fabric but a *covenant* with the very soul of backyard liberty.

It is with deep humility—and, I confess, a touch of existential dread—that I address the grave allegation that I own *zero* items of denim. Let me be unequivocal: **This is not a denial. It is a confession.** Yes, my closet is a denim-free zone, a sartorial Chernobyl where the very concept of rivets and indigo dye goes to die. I have no jeans. No jackets. No overalls (though I *did* once wear a pair ironically at a Halloween party, which I now realize was a mistake akin to bringing a tofu dog to a tailgate).

But let me assure this committee: **My lack of denim is not an act of subversion. It is a cry for help.**

I was raised in a household where the only "denim" was the faded blue of my father’s work shirts, which he insisted were "close enough." My first pair of "jeans" were actually khakis with a Sharpie-drawn fake Levi’s tag, a forgery so convincing that my middle-school gym teacher once asked if I’d "worn them to Woodstock." (I was born in 1992.) My high school prom date broke up with me when she discovered I had *no* denim in my wardrobe, not even a belt. "How can I trust a man who doesn’t own a single pair of 501s?" she asked. To this day, I do not have an answer.

I have tried, Chairman Brisket. Oh, how I have tried. I once purchased a pair of raw selvedge jeans from a boutique in Portland, only to realize I had no idea how to "break them in." I wore them once to a barbecue, and by the end of the night, they had fused to my legs like a second skin—specifically, the skin of a man who had just lost a bet with a deep fryer. I had to cut them off with trauma shears. The paramedic who treated me later testified before this very committee that my lack of denim was "a public health crisis."

But here is the truth, my fellow patriots: **I am not anti-denim. I am *denim-illiterate*.** My hands do not know the weight of a well-worn pair of Wranglers. My soul does not hum with the quiet pride of a man who owns more denim than he does silverware. I am a man adrift in a nation of denim enthusiasts, a lone wolf in a pack of wolves who all *own* wolf-themed denim vests.

Yet I ask you: Is this truly un-American? The Constitution does not mandate denim ownership. The Declaration of Independence does not list "thou shalt own at least three pairs of jeans" among its inalienable rights. Even our beloved cookout traditions—while enriched by denim—do not *require* it. I have grilled many a burger in sweatpants, and I daresay the meat did not suffer for it.

That said, I recognize the gravity of my situation. If this committee deems my denim deficiency a threat to the fabric of our society (pun intended), I am prepared to take corrective action. I will enroll in a denim rehabilitation program. I will attend a "Jeans Anonymous" meeting, where I will stand before a circle of my peers and say, *"Hi, my name is [REDACTED], and I own zero items of denim."* I will even submit to a supervised denim purchase, under the watchful eye of a committee-approved "denim mentor," who will ensure I do not accidentally buy *jeggings* (a crime against both denim and humanity).

In closing, I ask this committee to consider mercy. I am not a denim traitor. I am a denim *virgin*—a man who has never known the joy of a perfectly faded pair of Levi’s, the thrill of a denim-on-denim ensemble, or the quiet dignity of a man who can say, with pride, *"These jeans? I’ve had them since ‘Nam."* (I was born in 1992.)

I throw myself upon the mercy of the Cookout Division. And if mercy is not forthcoming, I ask only that my punishment be proportional. Perhaps a fine. Perhaps community service, in the form of folding denim at a Levi’s outlet. But please, I beg you—do not revoke my grill privileges. A man without denim may be pitied, but a man without grill access is truly lost.

**Thank you, and may your brisket always rest at 225°F.**

—[Your Name]
*Denim Deficient, but Still Patriotic*
